lead: A boundary layer normally clings to a surface and grows quietly along it. If the pressure starts rising in the direction of flow, the slow fluid near the wall runs out of momentum, stops, and turns back. The layer lifts off and leaves a churning wake behind it. That breakaway is separation. It matters wherever fluid meets a solid body: a bus on a highway, a chimney in monsoon wind, a bend in a water main, a cricket ball swung through the air, a wing at high angle of attack. Separation raises drag and can kill lift.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for how the layer grows, 5.3 for transition, and 5.2 for momentum thickness.

blocks.text: Pressure changes along a surface are set by the outer flow and pass almost unchanged through the thin layer. On the front of a cylinder or an aerofoil the flow speeds up and pressure falls: dp/dx < 0, called a favourable pressure gradient. Past the widest point the flow slows and pressure rises: dp/dx > 0, an adverse pressure gradient.

Rising pressure pushes fluid backwards, against the direction of flow. Fluid near the wall has already lost most of its momentum to friction. It cannot climb the pressure hill. It slows, stops, and then reverses. The layer lifts off the surface, and a wake with a recirculating eddy forms behind the body.

Watch the velocity profile. Near the leading edge the profile is full and steep at the wall, so the wall shear is large. Inside the adverse region the profile leans over and the slope at the wall falls. At the separation point the slope is exactly zero. Downstream it is negative, so the fluid touching the wall moves upstream.

blocks.where: τ<sub>w</sub> is the wall shear stress in N/m²; μ is the dynamic viscosity in Pa·s; u is the velocity at height y above the wall in m/s; y is measured in m. Separation needs dp/dx > 0 upstream of this point.

items: Find the outer pressure distribution and hence dp/dx along the surface.
Solve the layer, or the momentum integral, for u(y) at each station x.
Locate the station where (du/dy) at the wall reaches zero; that is the separation point.
Beyond it the layer equations fail; the wake must be measured or computed by CFD.

sections.h3: Friction drag, form drag and the coefficients

blocks.text: The fluid pushes on the body in two ways: shear along the surface, and pressure normal to it. Summing the shear gives friction drag D<sub>f</sub>. Summing the pressure gives pressure drag; after separation the wake holds low pressure, so the net pressure force points downstream. That part is form drag D<sub>p</sub>. Total drag D = D<sub>f</sub> + D<sub>p</sub>, in N.
C<sub>D</sub> = D / (½ ρ U² A)   and   C<sub>L</sub> = L / (½ ρ U² A)
blocks.where: C<sub>D</sub> and C<sub>L</sub> are the drag and lift coefficients, both dimensionless; D is drag in N and L is lift in N, the force perpendicular to the free stream; ρ is density in kg/m³; U is free-stream speed in m/s; A is a reference area in m², the frontal area for a bluff body and the plan area for a wing.

blocks.text: A flat plate parallel to the flow does not separate, so D<sub>p</sub> is nearly zero and all the drag is friction. The average skin friction coefficient uses the Reynolds number over the whole plate, Re<sub>L</sub> = UL/ν.

blocks.where: C<sub>f</sub> is the average skin friction coefficient, dimensionless; L is plate length in m; ν is kinematic viscosity in m²/s. The laminar form holds up to Re<sub>L</sub> of about 5×10⁵; the turbulent form is used above it. Then D = C<sub>f</sub> × ½ρU² × A<sub>wetted</sub>, with A<sub>wetted</sub> the total wetted area in m².

sections.h3: Delaying separation, and where lift comes from

blocks.text: Separation costs a low-pressure wake, which is expensive. Five practical remedies exist.

items: Streamlining: shape the rear so the pressure rise is spread over a long distance, giving the slow fluid room to recover. The classic teardrop.
Suction: draw the slowest fluid out through a slot, so fresh outer air reaches the wall.
Blowing: a small tangential jet near the wall injects momentum into the sluggish layer.
Vortex generators: small vanes that shed vortices which mix fast outer air down into the layer.
Trip wires and roughness: force turbulent transition early, because a turbulent layer carries more momentum near the wall and resists the pressure rise. Golf ball dimples work this way.

blocks.text: Lift comes from circulation. A body with circulation carries fluid faster over one side and slower over the other. By Bernoulli's equation the fast side has lower pressure, so a net force acts perpendicular to the free stream: that is lift. A wing gets its circulation from its camber and its angle of attack. Raise the angle too far and the adverse gradient on the upper surface becomes too strong, the layer separates, lift collapses and drag jumps. That is a stall.

figure.caption: The route from approach flow to a separated wake. Notice the two checkpoints in orange and green: a rising pressure gradient, then a wall shear that has fallen to zero, after which the flow near the wall turns back on itself.

spec.title: From attached layer to separated wake
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom chain from approach flow through an adverse pressure gradient and zero wall shear to separation and a rise in form drag.

examples.question: Air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s) flows at U = 10 m/s along a smooth flat plate 2 m long and 1 m wide, both faces exposed to the air. Estimate the drag on both sides (a) assuming the layer is turbulent from the leading edge, (b) assuming it stays laminar throughout. State which is nearer the truth for a real plate.
steps: Reynolds number over the plate: Re<sub>L</sub> = UL/ν = (10 × 2) / (1.5×10⁻⁵) = 1.33×10⁶, dimensionless.
Wetted area: both faces exposed, so A = 2 × L × b = 2 × 2 × 1 = 4.0 m². Dynamic pressure: ½ρU² = 0.5 × 1.2 × 100 = 60 Pa.

A real plate is laminar up to about 0.75 m and turbulent after that. A mixed-layer estimate gives about 0.74 N, so the true drag lies between 0.28 N and 1.03 N, closer to the turbulent value because the turbulent part of the plate carries most of the friction.
examples.answer: Turbulent from the leading edge: about 1.03 N. Laminar throughout: about 0.28 N. A real plate is laminar up to about 0.75 m and turbulent after; a mixed-layer estimate gives about 0.74 N, so the true drag lies between 0.28 N and 1.03 N, closer to the turbulent value because the turbulent part carries most of the friction.

L = 2.0

Re = U * L / nu
Cf_t = 0.072 / Re**0.2
A = 2 * L * b
D_t = Cf_t * 0.5 * rho * U**2 * A
Cf_l = 1.328 / Re**0.5
D_l = Cf_l * 0.5 * rho * U**2 * A

traps: A flat plate has two wetted sides. Using A = bL alone halves the drag; write A = 2bL when both faces touch the fluid.
The average coefficient needs Re<sub>L</sub> = UL/ν; the local skin friction at a distance x needs Re<sub>x</sub> = Ux/ν. Mixing the two gives a wrong C<sub>f</sub>.
Separation is not transition. Transition is laminar turning turbulent; separation is wall shear falling to zero under an adverse gradient.
Only dp/dx > 0 causes separation. A falling pressure gradient (dp/dx < 0) accelerates the fluid and keeps the layer attached. Watch the sign.
C<sub>f</sub> for a plate multiplies the wetted area; C<sub>D</sub> for a bluff body multiplies the frontal area. Do not swap the two areas.

quiz.q: State the wall condition that marks the separation point.
quiz.a: The velocity gradient at the wall is zero, so wall shear τ<sub>w</sub> = μ(du/dy)<sub>y=0</sub> = 0, and this happens where dp/dx > 0 upstream.

quiz.q: Why does a rising pressure gradient separate the layer while a falling one keeps it attached?
quiz.a: Rising pressure acts against the flow and decelerates the near-wall fluid, which has little momentum left after friction, so it stops and reverses. Falling pressure accelerates the fluid, keeps the profile full and the wall shear positive.

quiz.q: Why does a turbulent boundary layer resist separation better than a laminar one?
quiz.a: Mixing brings fast outer fluid close to the wall, so the profile is fuller, the near-wall momentum is larger and the wall shear stays positive longer against the same pressure rise.

quiz.q: Air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s) flows at 6 m/s over a smooth flat plate 3 m long and 1 m wide, turbulent from the leading edge, both sides exposed. Find the total drag.
A hoarding of frontal area 0.5 m² faces wind at 15 m/s (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) and feels 54 N of drag. Find C<sub>D</sub>.
Roughening a surface increases skin friction. Why can it still lower the total drag of a bluff body?
quiz.a: Roughness trips the layer into turbulence early. The fuller turbulent profile pushes the separation point rearward, shrinking the low-pressure wake. Form drag falls more than friction drag rises, so total drag drops. This is why golf balls are dimpled.

quiz.q: As a wing's angle of attack increases, the separation point moves forward. Explain what happens to lift and drag.
quiz.a: The adverse gradient on the upper surface strengthens, so wall shear reaches zero earlier and separation moves toward the leading edge. The wake widens, form drag rises sharply, and circulation weakens so lift falls. Past the critical angle this is a stall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern CFD closes the Reynolds-averaged equations with turbulence models such as k-ε and k-ω SST, and predicting the separation point accurately is still the hard part, especially near stall. Active flow control uses synthetic jets, plasma actuators and oscillating flaps to re-energise the layer on demand. Civil engineers fit helical strakes and splitter plates to chimneys and bridge cables because the regular vortex shedding that separation causes makes them vibrate; the strakes and plates break up that shedding. Riblets copied from shark skin and dimple patterns copied from golf balls are both attempts to buy a small drag reduction. Search for adverse pressure gradient, vortex generator, drag crisis and vortex-induced vibration to go further.
